sql:
SELECT z.LocationID, z.Borough, z.Zone, COUNT(t.PULocationID) AS cash_trips
FROM ops.zones z
LEFT JOIN lake.trips t ON t.PULocationID = z.LocationID AND t.payment_type = 2
GROUP BY z.LocationID, z.Borough, z.Zone
ORDER BY z.LocationID

SELECT z.LocationID, z.Borough, z.Zone, COALESCE(agg.cnt, 0) AS cash_trips
FROM ops.zones z
LEFT JOIN (
    SELECT PULocationID, COUNT(*) AS cnt
    FROM lake.trips
    WHERE payment_type = 2
    GROUP BY PULocationID
) agg ON agg.PULocationID = z.LocationID
ORDER BY z.LocationID

diagnosis.bottleneck: The query scans the full trips table (495k rows) to apply the payment_type=2 filter, then hash-joins the resulting ~99k rows to the 265-row zones table, and finally hash-groups those 99k rows into 265 groups.

plan_nodes.note: Join Type: RIGHT | Conditions: CAST(PULocationID AS BIGINT) = LocationID | Estimated Cardinality: 99167

hypotheses.claim: A filter on the joined side sits in the ON clause of a LEFT JOIN; the join dominates the cost. (matched: left join lake.trips t on … and t.payment_type = 2)

The sequential scan on trips reads all 495,833 rows because the columnar zone maps cannot prune row groups for payment_type=2 (only 5 distinct values, low selectivity); sorting or partitioning the data by payment_type would allow skipping irrelevant row groups.

The join condition uses CAST(PULocationID AS BIGINT) = LocationID, which adds per-row CPU overhead and may prevent the optimizer from using a more efficient join strategy; aligning the data types of PULocationID and LocationID would eliminate the cast.

The hash group by processes 99,167 joined rows to produce only 265 groups; pre-aggregating trips by PULocationID (and payment_type=2) before the left join would reduce the probe side to at most 243 distinct locations, cutting join and aggregation work dramatically.
